[[File:Modell einer Peanoschen Fläche -Schilling XLIX, 1-.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|right|Model of the Peano surface in the Dresden collection]]
In mathematics, the '''Peano surface''' is the [[Graph of a function|graph]] of the [[Multivariate calculus|two-variable function]]
:<math>f(x,y)=(2x^2-y)(y-x^2).</math>
It was proposed by [[Giuseppe Peano]] in 1899 as a [[counterexample]] to a conjectured criterion for the existence of [[maxima and minima]] of functions of two variables.<ref name="Emch">{{cite journal|last=Emch|first=Arnold|authorlink=Arnold Emch|doi=10.1080/00029890.1922.11986180|jstor=2299024|issue=10|journal=American Mathematical Monthly|mr=1520111|pages=388–391|title=A model for the Peano Surface|url=https://archive.org/details/jstor-2299024|volume=29|year=1922}}</ref><ref name="Peano1899">{{cite book|title=Differentialrechnung und Grundzüge der Integralrechnung|publisher=B.G. Teubner|year=1899|page=332|url=https://archive.org/details/differentialrec01genogoog/page/n348|first=Angelo|last=Genocchi|authorlink=Angelo Genocchi|editor-first=Giuseppe|editor-last=Peano|editor-link=Giuseppe Peano|language=German}}</ref>

The surface was named the Peano surface ({{langx|de|Peanosche Fläche}}) by [[Georg Scheffers]] in his 1920 book ''Lehrbuch der darstellenden Geometrie''.<ref name="Emch"/><ref>{{cite book|title=Lehrbuch der darstellenden Geometrie|year=1920|volume=II|first=Georg|last=Scheffers|authorlink=Georg Scheffers|contribution=427. Die Peanosche Fläche|contribution-url=https://archive.org/details/lehrbuchderdarst02sche/page/260|pages=261–263|language=German}}</ref> It has also been called the '''Peano saddle'''.<ref name="encyc">{{cite book|last1=Krivoshapko|first1=S. N.|last2=Ivanov|first2=V. N.|contribution=Saddle Surfaces|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-11773-7_33|pages=561–565|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]]|title=Encyclopedia of Analytical Surfaces|year=2015|isbn=978-3-319-11772-0 }} See especially section "Peano Saddle", pp. 562–563.</ref><ref name="Francis">{{cite book|last=Francis|first=George K.|isbn=0-387-96426-6|mr=880519|page=88|publisher=Springer-Verlag, New York|title=A Topological Picturebook|title-link=A Topological Picturebook|year=1987}}</ref>

==Properties==
[[File:Peano-flaeche-12.svg|thumb|upright=1.2|Peano surface and its level curves for level 0 (parabolas, green and purple)]]
The function <math>f(x,y)=(2x^2-y)(y-x^2)</math> whose graph is the surface takes positive values between the two [[parabola]]s <math>y=x^2</math> and <math>y=2x^2</math>, and negative values elsewhere (see diagram). At the [[origin (mathematics)|origin]], the three-dimensional point <math>(0,0,0)</math> on the surface that corresponds to the intersection point of the two parabolas, the surface has a [[saddle point]].<ref name="Fischer"/> The surface itself has positive [[Gaussian curvature]] in some parts and negative curvature in others, separated by another parabola,<ref name="encyc"/><ref name="Francis"/> implying that its [[Gauss map]] has a [[Singularity theory|Whitney cusp]].<ref name="Francis"/>

[[File:Peano intersection.png|thumb|upright=1.2|Intersection of the Peano surface with a vertical plane. The intersection curve has a local maximum at the origin, to the right of the image, and a global maximum on the left of the image, dipping shallowly between these two points.]]
Although the surface does not have a local maximum at the origin, its intersection with any vertical plane through the origin (a plane with equation <math>y=mx</math> or <math>x=0</math>) is a curve that has a local maximum at the origin,<ref name="Emch"/> a property described by [[Earle Raymond Hedrick]] as "paradoxical".<ref name="Hedrick">{{cite journal|last=Hedrick|first=E. R.|author-link=Earle Raymond Hedrick|date=July 1907|doi=10.2307/1967821|issue=4|journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]]|jstor=1967821|pages=172–174|series=Second Series|title=A peculiar example in minima of surfaces|volume=8}}</ref> In other words, if a point starts at the origin <math>(0,0)</math> of the plane, and moves away from the origin along any straight line, the value of <math>(2x^2-y)(y-x^2)</math> will decrease at the start of the motion. Nevertheless, <math>(0,0)</math> is not a local maximum of the function, because moving along a parabola such as <math>y=\sqrt{2}\,x^2</math> (in diagram: red) will cause the function value to increase.

The Peano surface is a [[quartic surface]].

==As a counterexample==
In 1886 [[Joseph Alfred Serret]] published a textbook<ref>{{cite book|first=J. A.|last=Serret|title=Cours de calcul différentiel et intégral|volume=1|edition=3d|location=Paris|year=1886|page=216
|url=https://archive.org/details/coursdecalculdif01serruoft/page/216/mode/2up|via=Internet Archive}}</ref> with a proposed criterion for the 
extremal points of a surface given by <math>z=f(x_0+h,y_0+k)</math>
:"the maximum or the minimum takes place when for the values of <math>h</math> and <math>k</math> for which <math>d^2f</math> and <math>d^3f</math> (third and fourth terms) vanish, <math>d^4f</math> (fifth term) has constantly the sign − , or the sign +."  
Here, it is assumed that the linear terms vanish and the [[Taylor series]] of <math>f</math> has the form
<math>z=f(x_0,y_0)+Q(h,k)+C(h,k)+F(h,k)+\cdots</math>
where <math>Q(h,k)</math> is a [[quadratic form]] like <math>a h^2+b h k+c k^2</math>,
<math>C(h,k)</math> is a [[cubic form]] with cubic terms in <math>h</math> and <math>k</math>,
and <math>F(h,k)</math> is a quartic form with a [[Homogeneous polynomial|homogeneous]] quartic polynomial in <math>h</math> and <math>k</math>.
Serret proposes that if <math>F(h,k)</math> has constant sign for all points where <math>Q(h,k)=C(h,k)=0</math> 
then there is a local maximum or minimum of the surface at <math>(x_0,y_0)</math>.

In his 1884 notes to [[Angelo Genocchi]]'s Italian textbook on [[calculus]], ''Calcolo differenziale e principii di calcolo integrale'', Peano had already provided different correct conditions for a function to attain a local minimum or local maximum.<ref name="Emch"/><ref>{{cite book|language=Italian|title=Calcolo differenziale e principii di calcolo integrale|first=Angelo|last=Genocchi|authorlink=Angelo Genocchi|editor-first=Giuseppe|editor-last=Peano|editor-link=Giuseppe Peano|publisher=[[Fratelli Bocca]]|year=1884|contribution-url=https://archive.org/details/calcolodifferen00peangoog/page/n234|pages=195–203|contribution=Massimi e minimi delle funzioni di più variabili}}</ref> In the 1899 German translation of the same textbook, he provided this surface as a counterexample to Serret's condition. At the point <math>(0,0,0)</math>, Serret's conditions are met, but this point is a saddle point, not a local maximum.<ref name="Emch"/><ref name="Peano1899"/> A related condition to Serret's was also criticized by [[Ludwig Scheeffer]], who used Peano's surface as a counterexample to it in an 1890 publication, credited to Peano.<ref name="Fischer"/><ref>{{cite journal|last=Scheeffer|first=Ludwig|date=December 1890|doi=10.1007/bf02122660|issue=4|journal=Mathematische Annalen|language=German|pages=541–576|title=Theorie der Maxima und Minima einer Function von zwei Variabeln|url=https://zenodo.org/records/2137054/files/article.pdf|volume=35|s2cid=122837827 }} See in particular pp. 545–546.</ref>

==Models==
Models of Peano's surface are included in the Göttingen Collection of Mathematical Models and Instruments at the [[University of Göttingen]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://modellsammlung.uni-goettingen.de/index.php?r=7&sr=32&m=443&lang=en|title=Peano Surface|work=Göttingen Collection of Mathematical Models and Instruments|publisher=[[University of Göttingen]]|accessdate=2020-07-13}}</ref> and in the mathematical model collection of [[TU Dresden]] (in two different models).<ref>[http://www.math.tu-dresden.de/modellsammlung/karte.php?ID=314 Model 39, "Peanosche Fläche, geschichtet"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200708083628/http://www.math.tu-dresden.de/modellsammlung/karte.php?ID=314 |date=2020-07-08 }} and [http://www.math.tu-dresden.de/modellsammlung/karte.php?ID=341 model 40, "Peanosche Fläche"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200709151804/http://www.math.tu-dresden.de/modellsammlung/karte.php?ID=341 |date=2020-07-09 }}, Mathematische Modelle, [[TU Dresden]], retrieved 2020-07-13</ref> The Göttingen model was the first new model added to the collection after [[World War I]], and one of the last added to the collection overall.<ref name="Fischer">{{cite book|editor-last=Fischer|editor-first=Gerd|doi=10.1007/978-3-658-18865-8|edition=2nd|title=Mathematical Models: From the Collections of Universities and Museums – Photograph Volume and Commentary|title-link=Mathematical Models: From the collections of universities and museums|year=2017|isbn=978-3-658-18864-1 }} See in particular the Foreword (p. xiii) for the history of the Göttingen model, Photo 122 "Penosche Fläsche / Peano Surface" (p. 119), and Chapter 7, Functions, Jürgen Leiterer (R. B. Burckel, trans.), section 1.2, "The Peano Surface (Photo 122)", pp. 202–203, for a review of its mathematics.</ref>
